title: Unit 2.2 Programming fundamentals — review and test
specPoints: Covers the whole of 2.2: variables and I/O, sequence/selection/iteration, operators, data types and casting, strings, 1D and 2D arrays, subprograms, files, records and SQL, random numbers
40 marks · 60 minutes · pseudocode or Python accepted · the in-page runner may be used for the programming questions if the teacher allows
Teachers: switch on Teacher view for the mark scheme and marking notes
learn: Demonstrate every construct in 2.2 in short written answers and in working code
Read code and state outputs accurately, including boundary cases
Write a complete short program from a brief, addressing every requirement
hook: Underline the command word. Count the marks. For 'write a program', list the requirements as bullets first and tick them as you go. For 'state the output', trace — do not guess.

list: `=` assigns, `==` compares. `input()` is a string. `int()` chops, `round()` rounds.
`for` when you know the count; `while` may run zero times; `do…until` runs at least once. OCR `to` is inclusive; Python `range` stop is not.
`MOD` remainder, `DIV` whole part. `and` needs both; each side a full comparison.
Strings and arrays index from 0; last index is length − 1. Python slice stop excluded; OCR `substring(start, count)`.
2D: row then column; nested loops; fix one index to total a row or a column.
Procedure does; function returns. Parameters in the definition, arguments in the call. Local variables die with the call.
Files: `w` wipes, `a` appends; everything read is a string; close the file.
SQL: SELECT fields FROM table WHERE condition [ORDER BY]; text in single quotes; `LIKE '%x%'`.
`randint(a, b)` includes both ends; call it inside the loop.

try.title: Scratch space for the programming questions
p: If your teacher allows it, write and run your answers to questions 7, 9 and 10 here, then copy them into the answer boxes.

exam.q: State the output of the following code.
exam.code:
x = 7
y = 2
print(x DIV y, x MOD y, x / y)
model: 3 1 3.5 (2 marks; 1 if two of the three are correct).

exam.q: State the most appropriate data type for each: a student's surname; the number of students in a class; whether a student is present; the average mark of a class.
State the output of the following pseudocode.
exam.commentary: substring(start, count): index 3 is g, four characters g-r-a-m.

exam.q: The following code is intended to output "Pass" for a mark of 40 or more and "Fail" otherwise. It contains an error. Identify the line and write the corrected line.
exam.code:
01 mark = int(input("Mark: "))
02 if mark > 40 then
03     print("Pass")
04 else
05     print("Fail")
06 endif

exam.q: Explain the difference between a count-controlled loop and a condition-controlled loop, giving an example of a situation where each is appropriate.
model: Count-controlled repeats a known number of times (1), e.g. printing every item of a list of 20 (1). Condition-controlled repeats until/while a condition holds, the number of repetitions unknown in advance (1), e.g. asking for a password until it is correct (1).

exam.q: State the output of the following Python code.
exam.code:
nums = [4, 9, 2, 7, 5]
total = 0
for i in range(1, 4):
    total = total + nums[i]
print(total)
print(nums[-1], len(nums))
exam.commentary: range(1, 4) excludes 4; nums[-1] is the last item.

exam.q: Write a function `average(numbers)` that returns the mean of a list of numbers, and show it being called with the list `[3, 5, 10]` with the result output.
model: Function header with one parameter (1). Loop or `sum()` producing the total (1). Returns total divided by the length of the list (1). Call with the list and output of the result (1).
exam.commentary: `return`, not `print`, inside the function; and the call line is a mark.

exam.q: A 2D array `seats[5, 8]` holds 1 for a booked seat and 0 for a free seat. Write an algorithm that outputs the number of free seats in row 2.
model: Counter initialised and loop over columns 0–7 (1). Checks `seats[2, col] == 0` — row fixed at 2 (1). Increments counter when free and outputs after the loop (1).

exam.q: The file `marks.txt` contains lines in the form `name,mark`. Write an algorithm that reads the file and outputs the name of the student with the highest mark.
model: Opens the file (1). Loops until end of file reading each line (1). Splits the line into name and mark and converts mark to a number (1). Compares with the current highest, storing the mark and the name when higher (1). Closes the file and outputs the name (1).
exam.commentary: Cast the mark; store the name alongside the mark; close the file.

exam.q: A table `Members` has fields MemberID, Name, Age, Town. Write an SQL query to display the names of all members under 18 who live in St Helier, in alphabetical order of name.
model: `SELECT Name` (1) `FROM Members` (1) `WHERE Age < 18 AND Town = 'St Helier'` (1) `ORDER BY Name` (1).
exam.commentary: Field named, both conditions with AND, quotes round the town, ORDER BY.

exam.q: A program needs to pick a random student from a list of 30 names to answer a question. Write pseudocode or Python to do this, and state one reason the programmer should ensure the same student is not picked twice in a row.
model: Random index 0–29 / `random.choice(names)` (1) and output of the chosen name (1). Reason: fairness / so every student is involved / to avoid one student being asked repeatedly (1).
exam.commentary: Index range 0–29 for a 30-item array; randint(1, 30) is an off-by-one.

exam.q: Give **three** reasons why a programmer should use meaningful variable names and subprograms in a large program.
model: Any three: easier for others (or the programmer later) to understand the code; easier to find and fix errors; code can be reused; parts can be tested independently; reduces repeated code (1 each).

teacher.timing: 60 min: review 10 · test 50. 40 marks. Feedback bands: 32+ secure; 22–31 developing; below 22 revisit lessons 3, 4, 8 and 10 before 2.3.
misconceptions: Use the marks lost per question to decide what to reteach: Q1–3 and Q6 are reading skills (trace more); Q7–10 are writing skills (more build time in 2.3).
say: 'Trace, don't guess. Tick the brief. Return, not print.'
teacher.skip: For a 45-minute slot drop Q5 and Q12 (7 marks) and mark out of 33.
differentiation: Support: allow the key-terms lists and the ten-minute review notes on the desk.
Stretch: Q9 — also output the average mark to one decimal place.
